questions.title: The Rover Ramp
text: Priya brought her rover to the robot fair at Harbor Middle School.
Her job was to drive it up a steep wooden ramp.
The rover rolled halfway up and then stopped.
Its battery was empty.
Priya groaned and put her hands on her head.
She had worked on the rover for three weeks.
She found a charger and plugged the rover in.
While she waited, she checked every wire.
Twenty minutes later, she tried again.
This time the rover climbed all the way to the top.
Priya smiled at Ms. Ortiz.
She had fixed it all by herself.
questions.question: Why do you think Priya felt proud?
questions.key: One good answer is: Priya felt proud because she fixed the rover herself. In the story, she checked every wire. Any honest answer is fine.

questions.title: The Heron
text: Early one morning, a tall heron walked slowly along the edge of a clear stream.
He was looking for breakfast, and the water was full of fish.
A small fish swam close to his long legs.
"That fish is far too small for a fine bird like me," said the heron, and he lifted his beak high.
Next, a young perch swam by.
"I will not open my beak for such a skinny fish," he said.
He decided to wait for a big, fat fish instead.
As the sun climbed higher, the fish swam away into the deep, cool middle of the stream.
The heron waited and waited, but no more fish came near the edge.
By noon, he was very hungry.
At last, he found a tiny snail on a rock, and he gobbled it up.
Then he thought about all the fish he had turned away.
He wished he had not been so picky.
questions.question: How did the heron feel at the end, and why?
questions.key: One good answer is: At the end, the heron felt foolish because he turned away good fish. Any honest answer is fine.

questions.title: The Broken String
text: Sam had been learning the guitar in the school music club since September.
In March, Ms. Gray invited him to play one song by himself at the library's Music Afternoon.
He practiced the song every evening for three weeks, until he could play it without looking at his fingers.
Even so, he had never performed alone in front of strangers, and just imagining it made his hands feel cold.
Twenty minutes before the show, Sam sat in a back room to warm up.
As he tightened one of the thin strings, it snapped with a sharp twang.
Sam stared at the loose string, and his face felt hot.
He had no spare strings in his guitar case.
Ms. Gray looked in her bag and found a new pack of guitar strings.
She helped him put the new string on, and together they tuned it.
She warned him that new strings stretch and can slip out of tune, and she told him to continue playing if that happened.
When Sam's name was called, he walked to the chair at the front of the room.
Grandma Rose was sitting in the second row, and she gave him a small wave.
Sam checked the new string one more time, took a deep breath and began.
Halfway through, the new string sounded slightly too low, but he continued playing, exactly as Ms. Gray had advised.
When he finished, the audience applauded loudly, and a small girl in the front row asked if he could play it again.
Sam laughed, and his hands did not feel cold anymore.
questions.question: At the end, Sam's hands did not feel cold anymore. Why do you think he felt better?
questions.key: One good answer is: Sam felt proud because he kept playing when the string sounded wrong. In the story, the audience applauded loudly. Any honest answer is fine.

questions.title: The Game Showcase
text: For six weeks, Ana and Leo built a video game together in the after-school coding club at Harbor Middle School.
In their game, a small robot named Bolt rolls through a city to deliver packages.
Ana designed the levels, and she spent most of her time on the last one, a maze of moving platforms that she had rebuilt seven times.
Leo wrote everything the characters said, and he filled the game with jokes, such as a grumpy mailbox that complained about getting too many letters.
At the end of the term, the club held a showcase, and anyone could come to the school gym to play the students' games.
For the first hour, Leo could hardly stop smiling.
Players laughed out loud at the grumpy mailbox, and one girl read every joke aloud to her little brother.
Ana, however, was watching the screen, not the players' faces.
Every player who reached the last level fell off the moving platforms within a minute, and most of them gave up and went to try another game.
After the fifth player walked away, Ana crossed her arms and stopped talking.
She wondered whether all her hard work on the maze had been a mistake.
Near the end of the showcase, a tall boy sat down and played the whole game without saying a word.
When he reached the maze, he fell off again and again, but each time he tried a different path.
On his twelfth try, he jumped onto the final platform and guided the robot safely to the last mailbox.
He threw both arms in the air and cheered so loudly that half the gym turned around.
Then he turned to Ana and asked whether she had designed the maze.
When she nodded, he said it was the best level he had played all day, because it made him think.
Ana uncrossed her arms, and for the rest of the afternoon she stood beside the screen, giving small hints to anyone who got stuck.
On the way out, Leo told her that people had laughed at his jokes, but her level was the part they would remember.
questions.question: On the way out, Leo said people would remember Ana's level. Why do you think he said that?
questions.key: One good answer is: Leo felt glad for Ana because he saw how upset she had been. Any honest answer is fine.

questions.title: Level Nine
text: Ben was stuck on level nine of his puzzle game.
He had to push ten blocks onto ten gold squares.
Every time, one block got trapped in a corner.
He tried for a whole week.
On Friday, he put down the controller and groaned.
Ana sat next to him and watched him play.
"Try moving the corner block first," she said.
Ben tried her idea.
This time, no block got trapped.
The last block slid onto the last gold square.
The screen flashed LEVEL COMPLETE.
Ben jumped off the couch and gave Ana a high five.
questions.question: Ben gave Ana a high five. Why do you think he did that?
questions.key: One good answer is: Ben felt thankful because Ana's idea worked. Any honest answer is fine.

questions.title: The Old Oak
text: For many years, a giant oak tree stood in the middle of Harbor Park.
Sam and his friends met under it after school.
Pixel liked to nap in its shade.
But the tree was very old, and its trunk was soft and weak inside.
Workers from the town said it had to come down.
On Monday, workers cut the tree down.
Sam stood by the fence and looked at the empty spot.
His eyes filled with tears.
He would miss the shade and the bumpy roots where he sat.
On Saturday, Grandma Rose came to the park with a small oak in a pot.
Sam, Priya and Leo dug a hole and planted it in the same spot.
Sam patted the soil flat.
"One day, this tree will be big too," he said, and he smiled.
questions.question: At the end, Sam smiled. Why do you think he felt better?
questions.key: One good answer is: At the end, Sam felt hopeful because the new tree will grow big one day. Any honest answer is fine.

questions.title: The Donkey and the Load of Salt
text: A merchant sold salt in a market town on the far side of a river.
Every week, he loaded heavy sacks of salt onto his donkey's back, and the two of them walked to market together.
On the way, they had to cross the river at a shallow place called a ford.
One morning, the donkey slipped on a smooth stone in the ford and fell into the water.
When he struggled back to his feet, the load on his back felt much lighter.
Much of the salt had melted away in the river.
The donkey trotted the rest of the way to market, feeling very pleased with himself.
The merchant was not pleased at all, because he had lost half of the salt he planned to sell.
On the next trip, the donkey remembered what had happened.
At the ford, he lay down in the water on purpose, and once again his load became light.
The merchant frowned as they walked on, and he began to think.
He guessed that the second fall had not been an accident.
The following week, the merchant filled the donkey's sacks with sponges instead of salt.
The sponges were light and dry, and the donkey felt sure that his trick would work again.
At the ford, he lay down in the river and waited.
But sponges do not melt the way salt does, because they soak up water instead.
When the donkey stood up, his load was far heavier than before, and he had to stagger slowly all the way home.
He never lay down in the river again.
questions.question: At the end, the donkey had to stagger home. How do you think he felt, and why?
questions.key: One good answer is: At the end, the donkey felt foolish because his trick did not work this time. Any honest answer is fine.

questions.title: The Weather Balloon
text: Every day, at hundreds of places around the world, weather scientists release large balloons filled with a light gas, such as helium.
Each balloon carries a small box of instruments that measures the temperature, the air pressure and the moisture in the air as it rises.
As the balloon climbs, the air around it gets thinner, so the balloon slowly swells until it bursts, often more than thirty kilometers above the ground.
Then the box floats back down on a small parachute.
In April, Ms. Ortiz's science class launched a weather balloon of its own from the field behind Harbor Middle School.
Priya had spent three weeks building the instrument box, which held a thermometer, a battery and a tracker that sent out its location every minute.
Sam had volunteered to follow the tracker on a map on the classroom computer.
At ten o'clock, the class counted down, and the white balloon rose quickly into the clear sky until it was only a dot.
For the next hour, Sam did not leave the screen.
He traced the balloon's path with his finger as the wind carried it east across the bay, and he called out its height every few minutes.
Priya stood behind him with her arms folded tightly.
The map showed the wind pushing the balloon toward the open sea, and if the box landed in the water, it would be lost along with all its measurements.
At 11:20, the height suddenly began to drop, which meant the balloon had burst.
The dot drifted lower and lower over the bay, and Priya held her breath.
At 11:58, the dot stopped moving.
Sam zoomed in on the map and laughed.
The box had landed in a cabbage field on Gull Island, only two hundred meters from the shore.
Priya let out her breath and sat down on the nearest chair.
That afternoon, Ms. Ortiz, Priya and Sam took the ferry across the bay, and the farmer met them at his gate with the box in his hands.
Back in class, Priya connected the box to the computer and found that the temperature high above them had dropped to fifty-five degrees Celsius below zero.
Sam printed the balloon's path and pinned it to the wall, and Priya stood in front of it for a long time.
questions.question: At the end, Priya stood in front of the map for a long time. Why do you think she did that?
questions.key: One good answer is: Priya felt proud because her box measured the air high above Earth. In the story, the temperature high above had dropped to fifty-five degrees Celsius below zero. Any honest answer is fine.

questions.title: Pixel Rings the Bell
text: Sam hung a small bell on the back door.
He wanted Pixel to ring it when he needed to go outside.
Every day, Sam showed Pixel the bell and gave him a treat.
For five days, Pixel just sniffed the bell and wagged his tail.
Sam sighed, but he kept trying.
On Saturday morning, Sam was eating breakfast at the table.
Then he heard a sound from the back door.
Ding, ding!
Pixel was sitting by the door, and the bell was still swinging.
Sam jumped up and opened the door.
"You did it, Pixel!" he shouted.
Then he called Grandma Rose to tell her the news.
questions.question: Why do you think Sam called Grandma Rose?
questions.key: One good answer is: Sam felt proud because Pixel learned the trick. Any honest answer is fine.

questions.title: Blue Sparks
text: On a warm summer night, Grandma Rose took Sam and Leo down to the beach after dark.
She had heard that the waves were glowing.
At first, Leo laughed and said it was probably just the moon.
Then a small wave broke on the sand, and a line of bright blue light ran along its edge.
Leo stopped laughing and stared.
Grandma Rose explained that the sea was full of tiny living things called plankton.
Some kinds of plankton make a flash of blue light when the water around them moves.
Sam waded into the shallow water up to his ankles.
Every time he kicked, blue sparks swirled around his feet.
Leo ran in next to him and pulled his hand through the water, making long blue streaks.
"It looks like a video game!" Leo whispered.
The boys stayed until Grandma Rose said it was time to go home.
On the walk back, Sam asked her if the plankton would glow again tomorrow night.
questions.question: On the walk home, Sam asked if the plankton would glow again. Why do you think he asked?
questions.key: One good answer is: Sam felt curious because he wanted to learn more about plankton. Any honest answer is fine.

questions.title: The Giant Footprint
text: Ben went to the museum with his class.
He saw a dinosaur footprint in a big rock.
Ben put his shoe next to the footprint.
The footprint was three times as long as his shoe!
Ben's eyes got big.
"Wow!" he said.
Then he took a photo of his shoe and the footprint.
He showed the photo to every kid on the bus home.
questions.question: Why did Ben show the photo to every kid on the bus?
questions.key: He was excited about the big footprint. Ben was excited about the big footprint. The photo showed his shoe next to a footprint three times as long.

questions.title: The Melting Ice Cream
text: It was a hot, sunny afternoon in Harbor Town.
Maya bought a cone of mint ice cream at the Lighthouse Café.
On the way home, she saw a sparkly rock next to the path.
She knelt down to look at it with her magnifying glass.
She looked at it for a long time.
When she stood up, green drops were running down her hand.
The hot sun had melted her ice cream.
Maya laughed and licked the drips off the cone.
Next time, she will eat her ice cream before she looks at rocks.
questions.question: Why did Maya's ice cream melt?
questions.key: The sun melted it while she looked at a rock. The hot sun melted the ice cream while Maya looked at a rock for a long time. Look at the first, fifth and seventh sentences.

questions.title: The Slippery Gripper
text: Priya's robotics club built a robot arm for the school science fair.
The arm had a gripper with two flat plastic fingers.
Its job was to pick up a tennis ball and drop it into a bucket.
On Monday, Priya tested the arm ten times.
The fingers closed around the ball each time, but the ball slipped out seven times.
Priya looked closely at the fingers.
They were smooth and shiny, so they could not hold the fuzzy ball tightly.
Sam, who was helping, said the motor could squeeze the fingers harder.
But Priya worried that a harder squeeze might crack the plastic fingers.
Instead, she wrapped a thick rubber band around each finger.
Rubber is soft and grippy, so it does not slide easily.
Priya tested the arm ten more times, and the ball slipped out only once.
At the science fair, the arm dropped every ball into the bucket.
questions.question: Why did Priya choose rubber bands instead of a harder squeeze?
questions.key: She worried that a harder squeeze might crack the plastic fingers. Priya worried that a harder squeeze might crack the plastic fingers. It is in the ninth sentence, just after Sam's idea.

questions.title: Rails in the Heat
text: Train tracks are made of long steel rails.
Like most metals, steel grows a tiny bit longer when it gets hot, and it shrinks again when it cools.
On a very hot summer afternoon, a rail in full sunshine can become much hotter than the air around it.
If a hot rail grows longer but has no room to move, it pushes sideways and can bend out of line.
Railway workers call this a "sun kink," and trains must slow down or stop until it is repaired.
Long ago, railways solved this problem by leaving small gaps between short rails.
Each gap gave the steel room to grow on hot days.
But the gaps caused new problems.
The wheels banged over every gap, which made the ride bumpy and wore out the wheels and the rail ends faster.
Today, many railways weld their rails together into one long, smooth rail with no gaps.
Before workers clamp the welded rail down, they warm it or stretch it, so it already has the length it would have on a warm day.
That way, it has much less need to grow when summer comes.
On the hottest days, some railways also paint the sides of rails white, because white reflects sunlight and keeps the steel cooler.
Trains may also run more slowly on very hot afternoons as an extra safety step.
questions.question: Why do some railways paint the sides of rails white?
questions.key: White reflects sunlight, so the steel stays cooler. White reflects sunlight and keeps the steel cooler. It is in the last paragraph.

questions.title: Reading the Weather Station
text: Every morning, two students in Ms. Ortiz's class read the school weather station and post a forecast by the front office.
This week, the job belonged to Sam and Maya.
On Tuesday, Sam arrived first, glanced out the window at a sky full of dark clouds, and wrote "Rain by noon" on the forecast card before Maya came in.
Maya hung up her jacket and went straight to the instruments: the rain gauge and the barometer.
The rain gauge from the night before was empty.
The barometer, which measures air pressure, showed the pressure rising steadily since dawn.
Ms. Ortiz had taught them that rising pressure usually means drier weather is on the way.
"Those clouds look heavy, but the numbers say they're moving out," Maya said.
Sam frowned at the card.
He had been sure, because the clouds looked exactly like the ones before last week's storm.
Still, he admitted that he had only looked at the sky and had not checked a single instrument.
Together they crossed out his words and wrote "Clouds clearing this afternoon," adding a small note that explained what the barometer showed.
By lunch, patches of blue sky had opened over Harbor Middle School.
Sam made a new rule for the rest of the week: read the instruments first, and look out the window second.
questions.question: Why did Sam make a new rule for the rest of the week?
questions.key: He learned that a look at the sky is only a guess, but the instruments give facts. Sam's guess from the clouds was wrong, but the instruments were right. So he decided to check them first.

questions.title: The Tall Tower
text: Sam, Ana and Ben played a block game at a table.
They stacked blocks to make a tower.
The tower got very tall.
Then Pixel ran under the table to get his ball.
His tail hit a table leg, and the table shook.
The tower fell down.
Everyone laughed.
Then they started a new game.
questions.question: Why did Pixel run under the table?
questions.key: To get his ball. Pixel ran under the table to get his ball. It is in the fourth sentence.

questions.title: Priya's Rover Stops
text: On Thursday, Priya took her rover to the park to test it on the grass.
She drove it in a big circle around a bench.
Then the rover slowed down and stopped in the middle of the path.
The little light on top had turned red.
Priya remembered that a red light means the battery is empty.
She had played with the rover all morning and forgot to charge it.
Priya carried the rover home and plugged it in.
After one hour, the light turned green, and the rover worked again.
questions.question: Why did the rover stop?
questions.key: Its battery was empty. The rover stopped because its battery was empty. The fourth sentence says the light turned red. The fifth sentence says a red light means the battery is empty.

questions.title: The Domino Run
text: On Friday after school, Leo and Maya built a domino run in the school library.
It had five hundred dominoes and went around two tables.
Mr. Hill said they could start it at four o'clock so the club could watch.
Ten minutes before four o'clock, a strong wind blew in through an open window.
It pushed a sheet of paper off a desk, and the paper slid into the last domino.
That domino hit the next one, and a long line fell backward.
Maya gasped, and Leo ran to the middle of the line.
He pulled out three dominoes to make a gap, and the line stopped falling at the gap.
Only fifty had fallen.
Maya closed the window, and they set the fallen ones up again.
At four o'clock, the club watched the whole run fall in a perfect line.
questions.question: Why did the dominoes start to fall early?
questions.key: The wind pushed a paper into the last domino. A strong wind pushed a paper off a desk, and the paper slid into the last domino. The fourth and fifth sentences tell this.

questions.title: Sunday Trip
text: On Sunday, Sam went to the train museum with Grandma Rose.
They saw a big black steam train.
Sam climbed into the driver's seat.
Then they rode a small train around the park.
Sam bought a postcard of the steam train.
He put it on his wall at home.
questions.question: What is this story mostly about?
questions.key: Sam's visit to the train museum The story is mostly about Sam's visit to the train museum. Every sentence tells something Sam did on that trip.

questions.title: Emperor Penguins
text: Emperor penguins live in Antarctica, where it is very cold.
They have many ways to stay warm.
Under their skin is a thick layer of fat.
Their short feathers are packed close together.
The feathers keep out the wind and the icy water.
On the coldest days, the penguins stand close in a big group.
This group is called a huddle.
They take turns in the warm middle.
Emperor penguins are the tallest of all penguins.
They dive deep under the ice to catch fish.
questions.question: What is this article mostly about?
questions.key: how emperor penguins stay warm The article is mostly about how emperor penguins stay warm. Most sentences tell one way: fat, packed feathers and the huddle. Catching fish and being tall are each in only one sentence.

questions.title: Saturday's Goalkeeper
text: On Thursday, Coach Novak had a problem.
The team's goalkeeper had a bad cold and could not play in Saturday's game.
Coach Novak asked Ben to play in goal instead.
Ben had never been the goalkeeper before, and he felt nervous.
On Friday, Ana kicked ball after ball at him during practice.
She told him to keep his eyes on the ball until it reached his hands.
By the end of practice, Ben's shirt was covered in grass stains.
The game started at ten o'clock on Saturday morning.
Ben stopped six shots, and the team won the game 2 to 1.
Afterward, Coach Novak asked Ben to be the backup goalkeeper for the rest of the season.
Ben's grass-stained shirt took two washes to come clean.
questions.question: What is this story mostly about?
questions.key: Ben learns to play in goal when his team needs him The story is mostly about Ben learning to play in goal when his team needs him. The kicks, the grass stains and the cold are each only one part of the story.

questions.title: Waiting for Launch Day
text: When a rocket is ready to launch, crowds often gather on beaches and roads nearby to watch.
Families bring chairs, snacks and binoculars, and some of them travel for hours to get there.
Yet many launches do not happen on the first day they are planned.
A launch that is called off for the day is known as a scrub.
Weather is one of the most common reasons for a scrub.
Strong winds high above the ground can push a rocket away from its planned path.
Some thick clouds carry electric charges, and a rocket flying through them could cause a lightning strike.
Engineers also watch readings from many sensors on the rocket, and if one reading looks wrong, they stop the countdown.
Each rocket also has a launch window, which is the period of time when it is able to leave.
Some launch windows last a few hours, but others last only a few seconds.
For the people watching, a scrub means more waiting.
Some families go home and return the next day, while others camp nearby.
Launch teams say that a scrub is a good decision, not a failure, because a safe launch matters more than a fast one.
When the rocket finally rises, many watchers say that the long wait made the moment even better.
questions.question: What is this article mostly about?
questions.key: Why rocket launches are sometimes called off, and how people handle the wait. It is mostly about why launches are sometimes called off, and how people handle the wait. The first paragraph says many launches do not happen on the first day, the second gives the reasons, and the third is about waiting. The other choices are single details.

questions.title: A Mine by the River
text: Copper is a reddish metal that is found in certain kinds of rock under the ground.
It carries electricity well, so it is used in phone chargers, computers, electric cars and the wires inside our homes.
To get copper, a company digs a mine, crushes the rock and separates the metal from the stone.
When a company plans a new mine near a town, people in the town often feel very differently about it.
Some people are glad, because a mine brings jobs that pay well, and the money helps local shops, schools and roads.
Young people who might have moved away to find work may be able to stay near their families.
Other people are worried.
Mines can be noisy and dusty, and big trucks carry rock along roads where children walk to school.
If waste from a mine leaks into a river, it can harm fish and the water that people and farms need.
Some people also love the forests and hills as they are, and they do not want them dug up.
Many people feel both ways at once.
A worker might want a job at the mine but also want to keep fishing in a clean river with her children.
To protect the land and water, many places have rules for mines.
In those places, a mine must test the water often, and when it closes, the company must cover the bare ground with soil and plant new trees and grass.
Before a new mine is allowed to open, people in the town can often go to public meetings, ask questions and share their views.
Hearing every side does not make the choice easy, but it can help a town make a choice that more people can accept.
questions.question: What is this article mostly about?
questions.key: How people in a town can feel different ways about a new mine The article is mostly about how people feel different ways about a new mine. The second paragraph says people often feel very differently, and the last paragraph says many feel both ways. Each other choice fits only one part.

questions.title: Three Days at the Skate Park
text: Leo wanted to learn a new trick at the skate park.
The trick is called an ollie.
In an ollie, you jump, and the board jumps with you.
On Monday, Leo tried it and fell off.
On Tuesday, he tried ten more times.
Sam sat on a bench and ate an apple.
On Wednesday, Leo and his board jumped up together.
He did his first ollie!
questions.question: What is this story mostly about?
questions.key: Leo learning to do an ollie The story is mostly about Leo learning to do an ollie. He tries on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. Sam's apple is only one small detail.

questions.title: Game Club News
text: Welcome to the October newsletter of the Harbor Middle School Game Club.
We meet every Friday from 3:15 PM to 4:45 PM in the school library.
Members can play board games, card games and video games on the club's two consoles.
Each console has a sign-up sheet on the wall, and each turn lasts 20 minutes.
Our big event this month is the Harbor Puzzle Cup on Friday, October 24.
Players will work in pairs to solve the puzzle levels in a game called Lighthouse Logic.
The pair that finishes the most levels in 30 minutes will have their names put on the club trophy.
To enter, write both names on the tournament sheet by Wednesday, October 22.
If you do not have a partner yet, write only your name, and Ben Diaz will help you find one.
Please remember the club rules.
Wipe your hands before you use a controller, because many people share them.
Put every game piece back in its box before you leave, and count the cards in each deck.
Use quiet voices, because other students are reading in the library.
Phones stay in backpacks during club time.
One more thing: the library is closed on Friday, October 17, for the book fair.
That day only, Game Club will meet in Room 8, and there will be no video games.
The consoles cannot be moved, but the board games and card games will be in Room 8.
See you on Friday!
questions.question: Maya wants to play in the tournament, but she has no partner yet. What should she do?
questions.key: Write only her name on the tournament sheet by October 22 Maya should write only her name on the tournament sheet by October 22. The second paragraph says players with no partner write only their name, and Ben Diaz helps them find one.

questions.title: Welcome, Junior Volunteers
text: Thank you for joining the Junior Volunteer program at the Harbor Town Animal Shelter.
Junior volunteers are 11 to 15 years old, and they help us care for the cats, dogs and rabbits that are waiting for new homes.
Every junior volunteer works with an adult family member, who must stay in the same room the whole time.
Shifts are on Saturdays and Sundays, from 10:00 AM to 12:00 PM or from 2:00 PM to 4:00 PM.
Please sign up for each shift on the paper calendar at the front desk at least two days ahead.
During your first three shifts, you will fold towels, wash food bowls and fill water dishes.
These jobs help the animals get used to you, and they help you learn how the shelter works.
After three shifts, you may also brush the cats and play with the rabbits in the small animal room.
Dog walking is only for volunteers who are 14 or older, because some of our dogs are large and pull hard on the leash.
Before you touch any animal, wash your hands at the sink by the door.
Wash them again when you move from one room to another, so that germs do not spread between the animals.
Never open a cage or a kennel by yourself; ask a staff member first.
Please wear closed shoes and clothes that can get covered in fur.
From December 1 to February 28, the afternoon shift moves to 1:00 PM to 3:00 PM, because the shelter closes earlier in winter.
Morning shifts stay the same all year.
If you cannot come to a shift you signed up for, call the front desk at 555-0172 as soon as you can, so that another volunteer can take your place.
questions.question: Sam signed up for a Sunday morning shift, but his family will be away that day. What should he do?
questions.key: Call the front desk at 555-0172 as soon as he can Sam should call the front desk at 555-0172 as soon as he can. The last sentence says this, so that another volunteer can take his place.

questions.title: Eclipse Day
text: Next Monday afternoon, the Moon will pass in front of part of the Sun.
This is called a partial solar eclipse, and Harbor Town will see it from 1:10 PM to 3:40 PM.
At 2:25 PM, the Moon will cover the biggest part of the Sun.
Lantern Peaks Observatory will give out free eclipse glasses at the library on Saturday.
Never look straight at the Sun without eclipse glasses, not even for a few seconds.
During a partial eclipse, part of the Sun is always uncovered, and its light can hurt your eyes.
Regular sunglasses are not safe, even very dark ones.
Before you use eclipse glasses, check them for scratches or holes.
If they are damaged, do not use them.
Put the glasses on before you look up, and look away from the Sun before you take them off.
Do not look through a telescope, binoculars or a camera while you wear eclipse glasses.
These tools gather the Sun's light and make it much stronger, so it can burn through the glasses.
If you do not have glasses, you can make a pinhole viewer.
Poke a small hole in a card, stand with your back to the Sun, and let the light shine through the hole onto a sheet of paper.
You will see a small, bright circle on the paper, with a dark piece missing where the Moon covers the Sun.
questions.question: Sam finds his eclipse glasses from last year. One lens has a tiny scratch. What should he do?
questions.key: Not use them, and get a new free pair at the library on Saturday Sam should not use them, and he should get a new free pair at the library on Saturday. The second paragraph says to check for scratches or holes and not to use damaged glasses. The first paragraph says free glasses are given out at the library.

questions.title: Calibrating the Rover's Distance Sensor
text: Priya's rover uses a distance sensor to stop before it bumps into a wall.
The sensor sends out a sound too high for people to hear, and then it measures how long the echo takes to bounce back.
Before each competition, the robotics club calibrates the sensor, which means checking that its readings match real, measured distances.
To begin, place the rover on a flat table with its sensor facing a cardboard box.
Use a ruler to measure exactly 20 centimeters from the front of the sensor to the box.
Next, connect the rover to the club laptop with the USB cable and open the program called SensorCheck.
Press the Read button three times, and write down each number that appears on the screen.
Now compare your three readings with the real distance of 20 centimeters.
If all three readings are between 19 and 21 centimeters, the sensor is accurate, and you can unplug the cable.
If the readings are all too high or all too low, type the difference into the Offset box and press Save.
For example, if the sensor reads 23 centimeters each time, the difference is 3, so you type minus 3.
Then press Read three more times to make sure your fix worked.
Sometimes the three numbers jump around instead, such as 15, 28 and 20.
Jumping numbers usually mean that the sensor is dusty or that the box is too small to send back a clear echo.
In that case, wipe the sensor gently with a dry cloth, move to a larger box, and start the whole test again from the beginning.
questions.question: Leo's three readings are 12, 30 and 21 centimeters. What should he do?
questions.key: Wipe the sensor, move to a larger box, and start the test again He wipes the sensor, moves to a larger box, and starts again. His numbers jump around, and the last paragraph says jumping numbers mean a dusty sensor or a box that is too small.

questions.title: Knife Rules at Cooking Club
text: Welcome to the Harbor Middle School Cooking Club!
This week, each team will chop vegetables for an enormous pot of vegetable soup.
Sharp knives are important tools, and a sharp knife is actually safer than a dull one, because it slices cleanly instead of slipping.
Always cut on a cutting board, never on a plate or in your hand.
Place a damp paper towel underneath the board so that it cannot slide.
Hold the food with your fingertips bent under, so the side of the blade touches your knuckles and not your fingertips.
This careful position is called the claw grip.
If a knife starts to fall, step back and let it drop, and never try to catch it.
To carry a knife, hold the handle with the blade pointing down, next to your leg.
Say the words "Knife behind you" when you walk past someone.
Never put a knife into a sink full of soapy water, because another person could reach in without seeing it.
Wash it separately, dry it carefully, and return it to the knife block.
questions.question: Priya finishes cutting. The sink is full of soapy water. What should she do with her knife?
questions.key: Wash it separately, dry it, and put it back in the knife block Priya should wash it separately, dry it and put it back in the knife block. The third paragraph says never to put a knife into a sink full of soapy water, because another person could reach in without seeing it.

questions.title: Fossil Dig Day
text: On Saturday, Dr. Bell and the museum team will lead a fossil dig for families at Shell Cliff Quarry.
The quarry's rocks formed on the floor of a shallow sea about 70 million years ago, when dinosaurs lived nearby.
Most fossils here are seashells, shark teeth and bits of plants, but last spring a visitor found part of a dinosaur's toe bone.
Every digger must wear a hard hat and safety glasses, which the museum will lend you at the gate.
Wear long pants and boots with closed toes, because the ground is covered with sharp stones.
Stay out of the area behind the orange fence, where the cliff face is loose and pieces of rock can fall.
Bring at least two bottles of water and wear sunscreen, since the quarry has no shade.
You may keep up to five shells or shark teeth that you find in the dig pile.
Any bone, and any fossil larger than your hand, belongs to the museum so that scientists can study it.
If you uncover something that might be a bone, do not dig it out yourself, because bones break easily when they are pulled from rock.
Instead, put a yellow flag next to it and call a museum worker, who will help you remove it carefully.
If your find is important, your name will go on its label when it is shown in the museum.
The dig runs from 9:00 AM to 1:00 PM, and children under 12 must stay with an adult the whole time.
If anyone sees lightning or hears thunder, everyone must walk back to the cars right away.
questions.question: Maya finds a small shark tooth. Then she finds a long, flat piece in the rock that might be bone. What should she do?
questions.key: Keep the tooth, put a yellow flag by the bone, and call a museum worker Maya should keep the tooth, put a yellow flag by the bone and call a museum worker. The third paragraph says you may keep small shells or shark teeth, that bones belong to the museum, and not to dig out a bone yourself.
